title: Honey never spoils.
explain: Sealed jars found in 3,000-year-old Egyptian tombs were still perfectly edible — its low moisture and acidity keep bacteria from surviving.

title: A shuffled deck is one of a kind.
explain: Fifty-two cards can be arranged in 52 factorial ways — a number vastly larger than the atoms estimated on Earth.

title: Water can be boiling and freezing at once.
explain: At its exact 'triple point' — one specific temperature and pressure — water exists as solid ice, liquid, and vapor all at the same time.

title: A metal exists that melts in your hand.
explain: Gallium has a melting point of about 29.8°C, just above body temperature, so a solid gallium spoon starts turning liquid the moment you hold it.

title: Hot water can freeze faster than cold water.
explain: Known as the Mpemba effect, it's been observed for centuries under the right conditions — and scientists still don't fully agree on why it happens.

title: The human body gives off a faint glow.
explain: Chemical reactions inside your cells produce a small amount of visible light, far too dim to see, but detectable with sensitive enough cameras.

title: Diamonds may rain from the sky — on other planets.
explain: Scientists believe the extreme pressure inside Neptune and Uranus can crush carbon into diamonds, which then sink slowly through the planets' interiors.

title: A neutron star is unimaginably dense.
explain: A sugar-cube-sized piece would weigh about as much as a small mountain — the result of a collapsed star crushed under its own gravity.

title: Sound can't travel through space.
explain: Space is a near-total vacuum, and sound needs molecules to vibrate through — without air, dust, or gas nearby, there's nothing for it to move across.

title: Your stomach relines itself every few days.
explain: Stomach acid is strong enough to dissolve metal over time, so your stomach replaces its protective mucus lining roughly every 3 to 5 days to avoid digesting itself.

title: Octopuses have three hearts.
explain: Two pump blood to the gills, one to the rest of the body — and that third heart stops beating when the octopus swims.

title: Wombats poop in cubes.
explain: The unusual shape keeps the droppings from rolling away once stacked up to mark territory.

title: Sharks are older than trees.
explain: Sharks have existed for over 400 million years — roughly 50 million years before the first trees appeared.

title: Sea otters hold hands while they sleep.
explain: They link paws in groups called 'rafts' so the ocean current doesn't drift them apart while they doze.

title: Tardigrades can survive the vacuum of space.
explain: These microscopic animals have been exposed directly to open space and radiation in orbit and revived afterward, unharmed.

title: Flamingos are born gray, not pink.
explain: Their signature color comes from pigments in the shrimp and algae they eat — without that diet, they'd stay a dull gray-white.

title: Bees can recognize individual human faces.
explain: Despite having a brain smaller than a grain of rice, honeybees can learn to tell different human faces apart in photos.

title: Elephants are the only mammal that can't jump.
explain: Their sheer weight and leg-bone structure mean all four feet can never leave the ground at once, unlike almost every other mammal.

title: A snail can sleep for up to three years.
explain: When conditions turn too hot, cold, or dry, snails seal themselves into their shells and enter a dormant state to wait it out.

title: Cows form close friendships.
explain: Studies have found cows kept with a preferred companion show measurably lower stress levels than when separated from them.

title: Lightning is hotter than the surface of the sun.
explain: A single bolt reaches roughly 30,000 Kelvin — about five times hotter than the sun's surface temperature.

title: Venus is the only planet that spins clockwise.
explain: Every other planet in the solar system rotates counter-clockwise, seen from above the sun's north pole.

title: A day on Venus is longer than its year.
explain: Venus takes 243 Earth days to rotate once, but only 225 Earth days to orbit the sun.

title: There are more stars than grains of sand on Earth.
explain: Astronomers estimate roughly a septillion stars in the observable universe — far more than the sand on every beach and desert combined.

title: Some dead stars spin 600 times a second.
explain: The fastest known pulsars — collapsed cores of exploded stars — rotate several hundred times per second, fast enough to blur past comprehension.

title: Saturn would float in water.
explain: It's the only planet in the solar system less dense than water — with a bathtub big enough, the whole planet would float.

title: The footprints on the Moon will last millions of years.
explain: With no wind, water, or atmosphere to erode them, the boot prints left by Apollo astronauts are expected to stay visible for millions of years.

title: Over a million Earths could fit inside the sun.
explain: The sun's diameter is about 109 times that of Earth, giving it enough volume to contain roughly 1.3 million Earth-sized planets.

title: A year on Mercury is just 88 Earth days.
explain: Mercury's tight, fast orbit around the sun means it completes a full year in less time than it takes Earth to finish three months.

title: Uranus rotates on its side.
explain: Its axis is tilted about 98 degrees, likely from an ancient collision — so unlike every other planet, it essentially rolls around the sun.

title: The shortest war on record lasted 38 minutes.
explain: Britain defeated Zanzibar on 27 August 1896, in what's recognised as history's briefest declared war.

title: The Great Wall of China isn't visible from space.
explain: Despite the popular myth, astronauts have confirmed it's not distinguishable with the naked eye from orbit.

title: Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the pyramids.
explain: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BC; Cleopatra ruled around 30 BC — closer in time to Apollo 11 in 1969 than to the pyramid's construction.

title: Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire.
explain: Teaching at Oxford began around 1096, while the Aztec civilization wasn't founded until 1325 — over two centuries later.

title: Woolly mammoths were still alive when the pyramids were built.
explain: A small population survived on Wrangel Island until about 1650 BC, overlapping with the early dynasties of ancient Egypt.

title: France used the guillotine the same year Star Wars came out.
explain: France's last execution by guillotine took place in 1977 — the same year the original 'Star Wars' premiered in theaters.

title: The first known recipe is nearly 4,000 years old.
explain: Clay tablets from ancient Mesopotamia, dated to around 1730 BC, record cooking instructions for stews — the oldest written recipes known.

title: Napoleon was once attacked by a horde of rabbits.
explain: During a staged hunting event in 1807, thousands of released rabbits swarmed his party instead of fleeing, forcing a retreat to his carriage.

title: The Eiffel Tower was almost torn down after 20 years.
explain: It was built in 1889 as a temporary exhibit with a 20-year permit, and was saved from demolition only because it proved useful for radio transmission.

title: Vikings never actually wore horned helmets.
explain: No genuine Viking-era helmet with horns has ever been found — the image comes from 19th-century opera costumes, centuries after the Viking age ended.

title: Bananas are berries. Strawberries aren't.
explain: Botanically, a berry develops from one ovary with seeds inside the flesh — bananas qualify, strawberries don't.

title: Carrots were originally purple, not orange.
explain: The now-familiar orange carrot was bred in the Netherlands around the 17th century; earlier carrots were typically purple, white, or yellow.

title: Chocolate was once used as currency.
explain: The Aztecs and Maya valued cacao beans highly enough to use them as money, sometimes trading a single bean for a small tamale.

title: Peanuts aren't actually nuts.
explain: They're legumes that grow underground, more closely related to beans and lentils than to tree nuts like almonds or walnuts.

title: White chocolate isn't technically chocolate.
explain: It contains cocoa butter but no cocoa solids — the part that gives chocolate its color and much of its flavor — so many definitions exclude it.

title: Apples float because they're 25% air.
explain: Roughly a quarter of an apple's volume is air pockets between its cells, which is enough to make it less dense than water.

title: Ketchup was sold as medicine in the 1830s.
explain: A doctor marketed tomato-based ketchup pills as a cure for indigestion and other ailments before it became a condiment.

title: Almonds are technically a seed, not a nut.
explain: An almond is the seed found inside the pit of a fruit closely related to peaches and plums — botanically closer to a stone fruit seed than a true nut.

title: Most restaurant wasabi isn't real wasabi.
explain: Genuine wasabi root is rare and expensive, so most sushi restaurants outside Japan serve dyed horseradish and mustard instead.

title: Vanilla is the second most expensive spice in the world.
explain: Because the vanilla orchid must be hand-pollinated and each pod cured for months, real vanilla is extraordinarily labor-intensive to produce.

title: Scotland's national animal is the unicorn.
explain: It's appeared on Scottish royal symbols since the 1300s, chosen for its associations with purity and strength.

title: Finland has more saunas than cars.
explain: With roughly 2 million saunas for a population of about 5.5 million, saunas are deeply embedded in daily Finnish life.

title: Denmark has a word for cozy contentment.
explain: 'Hygge' describes a feeling of warm, comfortable togetherness — there's no direct English translation, and the concept has become a lifestyle export.

title: Japan has more vending machines per person than anywhere else.
explain: There's roughly one vending machine for every 23 people in Japan, selling everything from hot coffee to fresh eggs and umbrellas.

title: Bhutan measures progress using happiness, not just GDP.
explain: Since the 1970s, Bhutan has used a 'Gross National Happiness' index alongside economic measures to guide national policy.

title: The shortest place name in the world is one letter.
explain: Several villages — including ones in Norway and Sweden — are officially named just 'Å,' a single Scandinavian letter.

title: The handshake may have started as a weapons check.
explain: One popular historical theory holds that gripping and shaking an open right hand showed you weren't concealing a weapon.

title: The depth of a bow changes its meaning in Japan.
explain: A quick nod signals something very different from a deep, held bow — the angle and duration communicate the level of respect or apology intended.

title: Vatican City is the smallest country in the world.
explain: At about 0.44 square kilometers, it's smaller than most golf courses, with a resident population of only a few hundred people.

title: Iceland has no mosquitoes.
explain: It's one of the only inhabited places on Earth where the insect can't establish itself, thanks to its particular climate and volcanic soil chemistry.
